Understanding Customers: Needs, Listening and Trust

Before you can sell well, you need to understand why people buy and how to find out what each customer really wants. This module covers customer needs, the questions and active listening skills that uncover them, and the basic protections (honest prices, safe payments, private data) that make customers trust you.

Customer relations means how you treat people before, during and after they buy. Sales means helping a person decide to buy something that is right for them. The two belong together. A trader who only pushes sales gets one purchase. A trader who builds relationships gets the same customer back again and again, plus the people that customer recommends.

Features, benefits and needs

Every product has **features**: facts about it. A blender has a 1.5 litre jar and a strong motor. A **benefit** is what the feature does for the person: she can blend pepper for the whole family in one go. A **need** is the real reason she is shopping: perhaps she sells food and grinding pepper at the market takes too long and costs her money. People buy to meet needs. Features only matter when you connect them to that need.

What customers weigh before buying
Most buying decisions, big or small, come down to four questions in the customer's mind, even if she never says them aloud.
What a customer weighs
Convenience: easy to buy
Trust: will she deliver?
Value: worth the price
Need: do I want this?
Need sits at the base: without it, good price and trust will not produce a sale.
**Need:** does this solve my problem or satisfy my want right now?
**Value:** is the price fair for what I get, compared with other options I know?
**Trust:** will this seller deliver what she promised, and will she help me if something goes wrong?
**Convenience:** can I buy easily, pay easily, and get it without stress?

Notice that price is only one part of value. Many customers happily pay a little more to a seller they trust, who answers WhatsApp messages quickly and delivers on time. That is why customer relations is not a soft extra. It is part of what the customer is paying for.
The value of a regular customer
Worked example: what one loyal customer is worth
For example, Ngozi sells pap (akamu) and moi moi from a stall near a bus stop in Enugu. One office worker, Chika, buys breakfast from her on most working days.
Chika spends about ₦1,200 each visit (approximate price).
She comes about 4 days a week, so about ₦4,800 a week.
Over about 48 working weeks in a year, that is ₦4,800 × 48 = about ₦230,400.
If Chika also brings two colleagues who each spend half as much as she does, that adds about ₦230,400 more.
One badly handled day (cold food, rude reply, wrong change) could lose all of this.
One regular customer, plus the people she brings, can be worth well over ₦400,000 a year to a small stall. Treating each customer as a long-term relationship is simply good business arithmetic.
Why customers stop coming

Most unhappy customers do not argue. They simply stop coming, and you may never know why. Common reasons include feeling ignored or treated rudely, a problem that was not fixed, quality that went down, prices that changed without explanation, slow replies, and a competitor who made buying easier. Each of these is within your control. The rest of this course gives you methods to prevent and repair them.
Needs that are not said aloud

Customers also have feelings attached to buying. A mother buying school sandals wants to feel she is providing well for her child. A man buying a gift for his wife wants to avoid embarrassment. A trader restocking from you wants to be sure she will not lose money. These emotional needs are real. When you notice them and speak to them gently ("These are strong, they will last the whole term"), the customer feels understood, and understanding is what turns a buyer into a regular.

In the Nigerian market, relationships have always mattered. Many traders already have their "customers" who come back for years, and those customers expect a little extra: a fair price without long haggling, a small bonus (the familiar "jara"), first choice of new stock, or patience on a bad day. This course turns those instincts into methods you can use on purpose, including on WhatsApp and Instagram where you may never meet the buyer face to face.

The fastest way to lose a sale is to start talking about your products before you understand the customer. A woman who walks into a fabric shop asking for "something nice" could be dressing for a wedding, a burial, a job interview or church. Each needs a different answer. Good sellers ask first and talk second.

Open and closed questions

A **closed question** can be answered with yes, no or one word: "Do you want red?" It is useful for confirming details. An **open question** invites the customer to explain: "What is the occasion?" Open questions usually begin with what, how, who, when, or tell me. Use open questions to learn, then closed questions to confirm.

Active listening in four habits
**Active listening** means paying full attention to understand the person, not just waiting for your turn to speak. It can be practised in four habits.
Active listening cycle
Attend fully
Ask open questions
Reflect what you heard
Summarise and confirm
Go round the cycle until the customer agrees you have understood her need.

**Attend:** put your phone down, face the customer, make friendly eye contact and give small signals that you are following ("Mm", "I see"). On WhatsApp, attending means reading the whole message, including voice notes, before you reply.
**Ask:** use open questions to understand the situation, the reason, the budget and the timing.
**Reflect:** repeat back the key point in your own words, including feelings. "So you have guests coming on Saturday and you are worried the food will not be enough."

**Summarise and confirm:** gather the details and check: "Let me be sure I have it right: jollof rice and chicken for about 40 people, delivered to Ikeja by 1pm on Saturday, budget around ₦150,000. Is that correct?"
Worked example: a tailoring enquiry on WhatsApp
For example, Halima runs a tailoring business in Kaduna. A new customer sends: "Hi, how much for a gown?"
Poor reply: "₦15,000." The customer may compare on price alone and disappear.
Halima instead replies: "Good morning, thank you for contacting us. I would love to help. What is the occasion, and when do you need it?"
Customer: "My sister's traditional wedding, in three weeks. I have the fabric already."
Halima reflects: "Lovely, congratulations to your sister. So you have your fabric and need a gown sewn in time for the wedding." Then asks: "Do you have a style in mind? You can send a picture."

After the picture, Halima summarises: "So: the style in the picture, your own fabric, ready by the 14th for a fitting, collection on the 18th. For this style the sewing charge is ₦18,000. Shall I book your measurement?"

By asking and listening first, Halima understood the deadline, the occasion and the style. Her price came with context, and the customer felt cared for, so price alone was no longer the deciding factor.
Listening mistakes to avoid
Interrupting to talk about your product before she finishes.
Assuming you know what she wants because of her age, dress or the last customer.
Correcting her or arguing about how she describes her problem.
Asking several questions in one breath, so she answers only the last one.
Replying to a long voice note with a one-word text that shows you did not listen.
Silence is allowed
After you ask a question, wait. Many sellers fill silence with more talking. A pause of a few seconds gives the customer time to think and often brings out the most important detail.
Four things to learn in every enquiry

A simple way to remember what to ask is to learn four things before you recommend anything: the **situation** (what is happening, who it is for), the **reason** (why now, what problem it solves), the **budget** (what she is comfortable spending), and the **timing** (when she needs it). Ask about budget politely: "So I can show you the best options, what range are you thinking of?" Most customers appreciate this because it saves them from the embarrassment of falling in love with something they cannot afford.

On WhatsApp, where many Nigerian small businesses do most of their selling, listening takes slightly different skills. Read the whole message and any earlier chat. Reply in the language and tone the customer uses, whether English, Pidgin, Yoruba, Hausa or Igbo. If she sends a voice note, listen to all of it, and if you need to reply by text, refer to what she said so she knows you heard it. Avoid sending your full price list as a first reply; ask one or two questions first.

Listening also helps you discover when you should not sell. If what she needs is not something you offer, say so and, if you can, point her to someone who does. That honesty is remembered, and it is one of the strongest builders of trust you have.

Customers return to sellers they trust. Trust grows from small, consistent things: prices that do not change mid-conversation, promises that are kept, money that is handled carefully, and personal details that are kept private. This lesson sets the safe foundation for everything else in the course.
A person making a payment on a mobile phone
Most sales now involve phone transfers, so safe payment habits protect both you and your customer.
Clear prices and clear terms

State the full price before the customer commits, including delivery, packaging or extra charges. If prices of your materials rise, tell customers before they order, not after. Write your terms in a short message you can paste: deposit, delivery time, what happens if she cancels, and how returns or corrections work. Nigeria's Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018 protects consumers from false or misleading representations, so honest, clear information is also the lawful way to sell.
Worked example: a clear terms message for a cake order
For example, Bisi bakes celebration cakes in Ibadan and takes most orders on WhatsApp.
Price: 2-layer 8-inch cake with name inscription, ₦35,000 (approximate, based on current ingredient prices).
Deposit: 50% (₦17,500) to confirm the order, balance on collection or before dispatch.
Order notice: at least 5 days before the event.
Delivery within Ibadan: ₦3,000 to ₦5,000 depending on area, stated before payment.
Changes: design changes accepted up to 3 days before the date. Cancellation after baking starts: deposit not refunded.
The customer knows exactly what she is paying and what to expect. Disputes become rare because the terms were agreed in writing before money moved.
Confirming payments safely

Fake transfer alerts are a common trick. A buyer shows a screenshot, or a text message that looks like a bank alert, and leaves with the goods. Screenshots and SMS can be faked. The only reliable proof is money you can see in your own account. Make it a fixed rule for yourself and anyone who sells for you, so nobody feels embarrassed to check. A genuine customer will understand; you can say politely, "Thank you Ma, let me just confirm on my app, it takes one minute."
Safe payment check
Customer says she paid
Open your bank app
Check balance and history
Amount and name match
Release goods
Never skip the bank app check, however busy or friendly the customer is.
Payment scam warning signs

Be careful when a buyer rushes you, sends a screenshot instead of waiting, claims the network is slow and asks you to release the goods now, overpays and asks for a refund of the difference, or asks you to send money to receive money. Confirm in your bank or POS app before handing over anything. For large orders, a payment link from a provider such as Paystack, or a business account with Moniepoint or Opay, gives you clear records.
Respecting customer data

Each phone number, address and order detail a customer gives you is personal data. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 sets rules for how personal data is collected and used, and the Nigeria Data Protection Commission (NDPC) oversees it. For a small business, the practical habits are simple:
Collect only what you need for the sale and delivery.
Ask before adding someone to your broadcast list or customer list, and remove them if they ask.
Do not share or sell customers' numbers to other traders or groups.
Do not post screenshots of chats or delivery addresses without hiding names and numbers.
Lock your phone with a PIN and keep your customer notebook somewhere safe.
Personal safety when meeting customers

If you deliver or meet buyers in person, meet in busy, public places where possible, tell someone where you are going, and do not carry large amounts of cash. Collect payment by transfer and confirm it before leaving the goods. Your safety matters more than any single sale.
Promises you can keep

Trust is also built or broken by promises. Saying "It will be ready tomorrow" when you know it may take three days wins the order but loses the customer. It is far better to promise a realistic time and deliver early. If something goes wrong, such as a supplier delay, power cuts that stop your work, or a dispatch rider who did not show up, tell the customer before the deadline, not after she has to chase you. A short message like "Good morning Ma, I am sorry, the fabric delivery was delayed, your gown will be ready Thursday instead of Wednesday. Is that still okay for you?" keeps her trust even with bad news.

Finally, keep records. A simple notebook or phone note with each order (name, item, price, deposit paid, balance, date promised) protects you if there is a disagreement and helps you keep every promise. You will build on this record in Module 3, where it becomes your customer list.

The Sales Conversation and Complaint Recovery

This module gives you a repeatable path for a sales conversation, from greeting to follow-up, and scripts for the moments that decide a sale: objections and closing. It ends with a clear method for handling complaints so that a problem becomes a chance to win the customer's loyalty.
The sales conversation, step by step

Present a recommendation using benefits linked to the customer's need
Offer a small number of clear options instead of a long list
Confirm the order details in writing

Good selling is not about clever talk or pressure. It is a helpful conversation with a clear direction. When you follow the same simple path each time, you stop forgetting important steps, you sound more confident, and customers find it easy to say yes. The path below works for a stall, a shop, a home business or a WhatsApp chat.
Two people having a business conversation
A sales conversation is a guided chat that moves from greeting to agreement.
The six-step sales conversation
Greet warmly
Ask and listen
Recommend with benefits
Answer concerns
Agree the order
Follow up
Each step prepares the next; skipping the listening step weakens everything after it.
Step 1: Greet warmly

Greet within seconds, use her name if you know it, and be genuinely welcoming. In person, stand up, smile and say good morning or good afternoon. On WhatsApp, reply quickly and politely. If you are busy, a quick "Good afternoon, thank you for your message. I am attending to a customer, I will reply you in 10 minutes" keeps her from moving on to another seller.
Step 2: Ask and listen

Use the skills from Module 1. Learn the situation, reason, budget and timing. Summarise and confirm before moving on. This step usually takes longer than beginners expect, and that is fine. A customer who has explained her situation to you has already invested time in you, and she will often prefer you to a seller who just sent a price.
Step 3: Recommend with benefits

Recommend one product, or at most two or three options, that fit what she told you. Too many choices make people hesitate and leave to "think about it". Use a simple pattern: **because you said... this one... which means...** For example: "Because you said the children are hard on their shoes, I recommend these leather sandals with stitched soles, which means they should last the whole term."

Offering good, better and best options lets the customer choose her level without feeling judged. Point out which one most people choose; it helps her decide. Show, do not just tell: let her touch the fabric, taste a sample, or see clear photos and short videos in natural light.
Step 4: Answer concerns

Most customers have a question or worry before buying: price, quality, delivery or trust. These are called objections, and they are normal. They usually mean she is interested. The next lesson gives you a method and scripts for them.
Step 5: Agree the order

When she shows signs of being ready (asking about delivery, colours, or how to pay), help her decide with a simple question: "Shall I prepare the medium size for you?" Then confirm every detail in writing.
Worked example: from enquiry to confirmed order
For example, Aisha sells wholesale and retail foodstuff from her shop in Kano and takes orders from customers across the city on WhatsApp. A customer, Ruth, asks about rice.
Greet: "Good morning Ruth, thank you for reaching out. How can I help today?"
Ask: Aisha learns Ruth runs a small canteen, cooks about 15 kg of rice a week, and cares about rice that does not break or turn sticky.
Recommend: "Because you cook in bulk and want firm grains, I recommend the 25 kg bag of the parboiled brand my other canteen customers use. It lasts you nearly two weeks."

Options: Aisha quotes today's price for the 25 kg bag from her written price list, and the price for two 10 kg bags if Ruth prefers smaller quantities. Rice prices change often, so she always checks her latest supplier price first.

Agree: Ruth picks the 25 kg bag. Aisha sends: "Order: 1 × 25 kg parboiled rice, price as quoted today, delivery to Sabon Gari tomorrow before 10am, ₦1,500 delivery. Please pay to [business account] and I will confirm on my app."
Every step had a purpose. Ruth bought what fit her canteen, the written confirmation prevented confusion, and Aisha now knows Ruth's weekly usage, which makes a follow-up offer easy in two weeks.
Step 6: Follow up

After delivery, send a short check-in within a day or two: "Good afternoon Ruth, I hope the rice arrived well. Is the quality what you wanted?" This takes thirty seconds and catches problems early. It also makes the next sale feel natural. Module 4 covers follow-up and loyalty in more depth.

Handling objections and closing without pressure

An objection is any reason a customer gives for not buying yet: "It is too expensive", "Let me think about it", "How do I know it is original?" Many sellers hear an objection as rejection and either give up or start arguing. Both lose the sale. An objection is really a request for more information or reassurance.
Two people talking through a question
Treat objections as questions to be answered calmly, not as arguments to win.
A four-step method for any objection
Handling an objection
Acknowledge the concern
Clarify what she means
Respond with facts
Check she is satisfied
Clarifying first stops you answering the wrong worry.
**Acknowledge:** show you understand, without agreeing that the product is bad. "I understand, you want to be sure it is worth the money."
**Clarify:** ask what exactly worries her. "Is it the total price, or are you comparing with another one you saw?"
**Respond:** give a short, honest answer with facts, a sample, a guarantee or an alternative.
**Check:** "Does that answer your concern?" If yes, move towards the order. If not, go round again.

Dropping your price the moment someone says 'too expensive' teaches customers to always push, and it eats your profit. First clarify and explain value. If you do adjust, change something in return, such as a smaller size, simpler packaging or collecting instead of delivery.
Haggling with respect

Price negotiation is normal in many Nigerian markets. Know your numbers before you start: your cost, your normal price and your lowest acceptable price. Never go below your lowest price just to win the sale; a sale at a loss is not a success. Many experienced traders start a little above their target to leave room, but very high starting prices damage trust, especially with online customers who compare quickly. For regulars, consider a fair fixed "customer price" that saves you both the stress.
Worked example: handling a price objection on WhatsApp
For example, Funmi sells hair extensions online from Port Harcourt. A customer says her 18-inch bundle at ₦45,000 (approximate price) is too costly because she saw one for ₦30,000.
Acknowledge: "I understand, ₦15,000 difference is a lot."
Clarify: "Was the other one the same type, human hair, and the same weight?" The customer is not sure.

Respond: "Mine is 100% human hair, which you can wash, curl and reuse for many months. Many cheaper ones are synthetic blends that tangle quickly. I can send you a short video of the bundle being washed and straightened."
Offer a fair option: "If the budget is tight, my 14-inch in the same quality is ₦36,000."
Check: "Which works better for you?" The customer chooses the 14-inch.
Funmi kept her price honest, educated the customer on the real difference, and offered a cheaper option by changing the product, not by cutting her margin.
Buying signals and closing

**Closing** simply means helping the customer make the decision. Watch for buying signals: she asks about delivery, payment, sizes or colours, says "my sister would like this", or keeps holding the item. When you see these, ask a simple, low-pressure question:
Choice close: "Would you like the blue or the green?"
Next-step close: "Shall I send you the account details?"
Summary close: "So that is two packs of the shea butter and one black soap, delivered Friday. Shall I go ahead?"

If the answer is no, accept it warmly: "No problem at all, thank you for checking with me. Can I message you when new stock arrives?" A polite no today often becomes a yes later, and pressure would have closed that door. Avoid tricks such as false deadlines ("only today") when they are not true; you will meet these again in the ethics lesson.

Every business gets complaints: a late delivery, a wrong size, a cake that arrived damaged, a product that did not work. The complaint itself is rarely what loses the customer. What decides whether she comes back is how you handle it. Handled well, a complaint can leave a customer more loyal than before, because she has seen that you stand behind what you sell.
A support person helping a customer
A calm, structured response turns an unhappy customer into a loyal one.
The LAST method
LAST is a simple, widely taught customer service method. Its four letters are easy to remember when you are under pressure.
LAST complaint recovery
Listen fully
Apologise sincerely
Solve the problem
Thank the customer
Follow the order: solving before listening usually makes the customer angrier.

**Listen:** let her explain fully without interrupting or defending yourself. Take notes. Ask questions to understand exactly what happened: what she ordered, what she received, when, and what she would like now.

**Apologise:** say sorry for her experience, sincerely and without excuses. "I am truly sorry the cake arrived damaged, especially on your son's birthday." An apology is not an admission that she is right about everything; it shows you care about how she feels.

**Solve:** offer a fair fix, or ask her what would make it right, and agree on it. Then do what you promised, quickly. Common fixes are a replacement, a repair or alteration, a partial refund, a full refund, or a credit for her next order.
**Thank:** thank her for telling you. "Thank you for letting me know; it helps me improve." Then follow up after the fix to check she is satisfied.

Worked example: a weekly service check
For example, Grace runs a small skincare shop in Abuja and sells mostly on WhatsApp. Every Saturday evening she spends 20 minutes checking her five standards.

Accuracy: one order went out with the wrong size of body butter. It was confirmed in writing, so the mistake happened at packing.
Delivery: two deliveries were delayed; she warned one customer early but forgot the other.

Ask customers directly

Every few weeks, ask a few customers one simple question: "On a scale of 1 to 10, how likely are you to recommend us to a friend, and what is one thing we could do better?" Write the answers in your notebook. The suggestions are often more useful than the score.

If someone helps you, such as a sales assistant, a family member or a dispatch rider, share your standards with them in writing and explain why each one matters. Then check gently and praise them when they get it right. Your customers experience your business through everyone who serves them.

Standards also protect you. Many small business owners answer messages at midnight and feel exhausted, then serve customers poorly the next day. If you offer something outside your normal hours, such as an urgent same-day order, you can charge a fair extra fee and say so clearly before the customer agrees.

Review your standards every few months. As your business grows, you may be able to promise more, such as faster delivery or longer opening hours. When you cannot keep a standard any longer, change it openly rather than quietly failing it. A smaller promise kept is better than a big promise broken.

Consumer protection in Nigeria

The **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Act (FCCPA) 2018** is Nigeria's main consumer protection law, and the **Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission (FCCPC)** enforces it and receives consumer complaints. In plain terms, the law expects businesses to give consumers accurate information, to avoid false or misleading claims about goods and services, to supply goods of reasonable quality that match their description, and to deal fairly with customers. For products that are regulated, such as food, drinks, cosmetics and medicines, **NAFDAC** registration rules also apply, and the **Standards Organisation of Nigeria (SON)** sets standards for many other products.
This is general guidance

This lesson explains principles, not the full law. If you face a specific legal question, such as a large dispute or a product registration issue, check the official FCCPC or NAFDAC websites or ask a qualified adviser.
Claims to avoid

**Health and cure claims:** do not say a cream, tea, soap or supplement cures, treats or prevents a disease (for example "cures eczema" or "cures infertility"). These are medical claims, and products making them fall under strict NAFDAC rules.
**False origin or brand claims:** do not call a product "original", "imported from UK" or by a famous brand name unless you are sure it is true.
**Fake scarcity or deadlines:** "Only 2 left!" or "Price goes up tonight!" when it is not true.
**Edited or borrowed photos:** using someone else's pictures, or heavily filtered ones, so the product looks better than it is.
**Fake reviews:** writing reviews yourself or asking friends to praise products they never used.
**Hidden charges:** adding delivery or packaging fees only after payment.
Worked example: rewriting a misleading post

For example, Comfort makes natural body creams in Benin City. Her first Instagram caption read: "Miracle cream! Cures eczema and removes all dark spots in 3 days. Only 5 jars left, price doubles tomorrow!"
She checks each claim. She has no proof it cures eczema, and a cure claim is a medical claim.
"All dark spots in 3 days" is an exaggeration she cannot guarantee.
She actually has 40 jars, and the price is not changing.

She rewrites: "Rich shea and cocoa butter cream for dry skin. Customers like how soft their skin feels in harmattan. 250 g jar, ₦6,500 (approximate). Delivery in Benin City ₦1,500. Patch test first if you have sensitive skin."
She adds a real photo of the jar and a real customer comment shared with permission.
The new post is honest, specific and still attractive. It describes true benefits, sets fair expectations and avoids medical claims that could cause harm or regulatory trouble.
Fair pricing and fair treatment

Ethical selling also means treating customers fairly. Charge the same posted price to everyone for the same item, or be open about what changes it (quantity, delivery distance). Do not take advantage of someone who seems desperate or who does not understand the product well. Do not push a more expensive item that does not fit her need. Keep your word on refunds and returns according to the terms you stated.
Honest reviews and testimonials

Reviews from real customers are powerful because other buyers trust them more than your own words. Collect them honestly: ask satisfied customers if they would share a short comment, and ask permission before you post their message or photo. Hide their phone number and, if they prefer, their name. Never edit a review to say something the customer did not say, and do not hide every negative comment. A page with only perfect praise can look less believable than one that shows a calm, helpful reply to a problem.

Be honest about yourself too. If you resell products rather than make them, do not claim they are handmade by you. If a product is a cheaper alternative to a famous brand, describe it by its own name and qualities. Customers forgive a lower price point far more readily than they forgive feeling deceived.
A quick ethics test
**Is it true?** Can you prove every claim you make?
**Is it fair?** Would you be happy if a seller treated your mother this way?
**Would you say it in public?** If this message were shown to your whole church or market association, would you be comfortable?
**Will she still be happy next month?** A good sale leaves the customer satisfied after using the product, not just at the moment she pays.

Simple loyalty rewards
A loyalty reward thanks regular customers and gives them a reason to keep choosing you. It should be simple, affordable for you, and clearly explained. Work out the cost before you offer it.
**Stamp card:** buy 5, get a small free item or discount on the 6th. Paper cards work, or track it in your customer list.

Worked example: costing a stamp card
For example, Ngozi sells breakfast at her Enugu stall. Her average order is about ₦1,200, and her cost for one serving is about ₦700 (approximate figures).
She considers: buy 9 breakfasts, get the 10th free.
Sales from 9 paid breakfasts: 9 × ₦1,200 = ₦10,800. Cost of 10 breakfasts: 10 × ₦700 = ₦7,000.
Profit over the 10 breakfasts: ₦10,800 − ₦7,000 = ₦3,800, compared with ₦5,000 profit for 10 paid ones (10 × ₦500).
So each completed card costs her about ₦1,200 of profit, about 11% of the ₦10,800 that customer spent.
She decides it is worth it if the card makes customers choose her stall over the one across the road, and she will review it after 2 months by counting how many cards are active.
Ngozi knows exactly what the reward costs and how she will judge whether it works, instead of guessing.

Where referrals come from

Look at the "How she found you" column in your customer list. It shows which customers and which places bring you new business. Where you are welcome, a respectful introduction or a sample at a meeting can start a chain of recommendations. Referrals also depend on how you treat the new customer. She arrives with the expectation her friend gave her. Your thank-you should reward genuine customers who bought what they needed.

Worked example: a 90-day plan

Customer relations means how you treat people before, during and after they buy.

Every product has features. A feature is a fact about it. For example, this shea butter is unrefined.
A benefit is what that feature does for the person. Unrefined shea butter keeps its natural moisturising quality.
A need is the real reason she is shopping. Perhaps her child has dry skin in harmattan.

In her mind
Four things every customer weighs
Need: does this solve my problem now?
Value: is the price fair for what I get?
Trust: will this seller deliver and help me?
Convenience: can I buy and pay without stress?
Most buying decisions come down to four questions, even if she never says them aloud. First, need. Without it, good price and trust will not produce a sale.
Second, value. Is the price fair compared with other options she knows? Price is only one part of value.
Third, trust. Will you deliver what you promised, and help her if something goes wrong?
Fourth, convenience. Can she buy, pay and receive it easily?
Many customers pay a little more to a seller who answers quickly and delivers on time.

Here is why this matters in money. Ngozi sells pap and moi moi from a stall in Enugu. An office worker, Chika, buys breakfast from her on most working days.

Step by step
Ask first, talk second. Confirm her need before you recommend.
Attend: phone down, face her, read the whole message
Ask: open questions about situation, reason, budget, timing
Reflect: repeat the key point in your own words
Summarise and confirm: check you have it right
Active listening means paying full attention to understand her, not just waiting for your turn to speak.
Habit one, attend. Put your phone down and face her. On WhatsApp, read the whole message and listen to the whole voice note before you reply.
Habit two, ask. Use open questions that begin with what, how, who or when. Instead of asking, do you want a cake, ask, what kind of celebration are you planning?
Habit three, reflect. Repeat back the key point, including feelings. So you have guests coming on Saturday and you are worried the food will not be enough.
Habit four, summarise and confirm. Gather the details and ask, is that correct?

Good selling is not about clever talk or pressure. It is a helpful conversation with a clear direction.

Step by step
Because you said... this one... which means...
Recommend with benefits: one to three options
Agree the order in writing
Follow up after delivery
Step one, greet warmly, within seconds. If you are busy, say you will reply in 10 minutes, so she does not move on.
Step two, ask and listen. Learn the situation, reason, budget and timing, then summarise and confirm.
Step three, recommend one product, or at most two or three options. Too many choices make people hesitate and leave to think about it.
Use this pattern. Because you said the children are hard on their shoes, I recommend these leather sandals with stitched soles, which means they should last the whole term.
Step four, answer her concerns. We will look at these next.
Step five, when she asks about delivery or how to pay, help her decide. Shall I prepare the medium size for you? Then confirm every detail in writing.
Step six, follow up within a day or two. I hope the rice arrived well. It takes thirty seconds and catches problems early.
Objections
Four steps for any objection
Do not answer price with an immediate discount.
Respond with facts, a sample or an option
An objection is any reason she gives for not buying yet. It usually means she is interested and wants more information. First, acknowledge. I understand, you want to be sure it is worth the money.
Second, clarify. Is it the total price, or are you comparing with another one you saw? Clarifying first stops you answering the wrong worry.
Third, respond with a short, honest answer: facts, a sample, a guarantee or an alternative.
Fourth, check. Does that answer your concern?

The common mistake is dropping your price the moment someone says too expensive. It teaches customers to always push, and it eats your profit. Know your cost, your normal price and your lowest price before you start.

A price objection on WhatsApp
For example, Funmi sells hair extensions online from Port Harcourt.
Naira prices are approximate.
Her 18-inch human hair bundle
Bundle the customer saw
Her 14-inch, same quality
Here is the method in action. Funmi sells hair extensions online from Port Harcourt.
A customer says her 18-inch bundle at 45,000 naira is too costly, because she saw one for 30,000.
Funmi acknowledges the concern, then clarifies: was the other one human hair, and the same weight? The customer is not sure.
Funmi explains that hers is 100% human hair you can wash and reuse for many months.
Then she offers her 14-inch in the same quality for 36,000. The customer chooses it. Funmi changed the product, not her margin.
Complaints
The LAST recovery method
Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank. In that order.
Listen fully, without defending yourself
Apologise sincerely, without excuses
Solve: agree a fair fix and do it fast
Thank her, then follow up
Every business gets complaints. What decides whether she comes back is how you handle it. L, listen. Let her explain fully without interrupting.
A, apologise sincerely. When Bisi's cake arrived in Ibadan with the top layer cracked, she said: I am so sorry, this is not the cake you paid for.
S, solve. Bisi decorated a plain 8-inch cake from stock, sent it by car within 90 minutes, free, and refunded 10,000 naira of the 35,000.
T, thank. Thank you for your patience today. Then Bisi fixed the cause: tiered cakes now go only by car.
Follow the order. Solving before listening usually makes the customer angrier.

What to say instead
Avoid
It is not my fault
You should have checked
Calm down
Going silent
Say instead
Let me see how I can fix this
Thank you for sending the photos
I want to make it right
Reply within the hour

Say instead, let me see how I can fix this for you. Thank you for sending the photos. I want to make it right. And reply within the hour.
If she complains in public, reply once, calmly, and move to a private chat.

Remember
Greet, ask, recommend, answer, agree, follow up
Value first; never sell below your lowest price

Is it fair? Would you treat your mother this way?
Would you say it in public?
Will she still be happy next month?

Referred customers arrive already trusting you
A small plan kept for 90 days changes a business
Most of the hard work in sales happens before the first purchase. Once a customer has bought and been happy, selling to her again is much easier.
Yet many small businesses never contact a customer again after delivery.
A happy customer can also recommend you. Someone she knows arrives already trusting you a little.
In this video you will plan follow-ups, a loyalty reward, referrals, and a 90-day plan.
Step by step
A follow-up after every sale
Each message has a purpose. None is a hard sales push.
Day 2: satisfaction check
Before she runs out: reorder reminder
Special dates: a short personal greeting
Day 0, say thank you. Thank you for your order, Ada. It was a pleasure serving you.
Day 2, check satisfaction. I hope the shea butter is working well for you. This catches problems early, when they are easy to fix.
Then a reorder reminder, timed for just before she runs out. Ask customers how long the product lasted, note it, and put the next follow-up date in your list.
Now and then, a festive greeting, kept personal and brief.
Do not overdo messages. Too many promotions make customers mute or block you, and never add people to groups without asking.
Worked example
Costing a stamp card
For example, Ngozi sells breakfast at her Enugu stall. Buy 9, get the 10th free.
Naira prices are approximate.

Always cost a loyalty reward before you offer it. Ngozi's average order is about 1,200 naira, and one serving costs her about 700. She considers: buy 9 breakfasts, get the 10th free.
9 paid breakfasts bring 10,800 naira. 10 breakfasts cost her 7,000.
So her profit is 3,800 naira, compared with 5,000 for 10 paid ones.
Each completed card costs her about 1,200 naira of profit. She decides it is worth it if customers choose her stall over the one across the road, and she will review it after 2 months.
Referrals
Thank referrers modestly. Avoid schemes built on recruiting.
Make sharing easy: a message to forward
Ask for a referral right after she shows she is happy. Halima's customer sent a wedding photo: everybody asked who sewed my gown!
Halima thanked her, and asked permission before sharing the photo.
Then she asked a specific question: if any of the ladies would like an outfit, I would be happy to help.
She made it easy, with a short message to forward: her value statement and how to order.
When a new customer mentioned the referrer, Halima thanked her with a small discount on her next order.
Keep thank-yous modest. Schemes built on recruiting people rather than real sales can be pyramid schemes, which harm the people who join late.
With permission
Testimonials done right
Ask permission before posting
Hide phone numbers, and names if she prefers
Use her real words, unedited
Prefer specific praise over vague praise

Real customer words are powerful, so collect them honestly. Ask permission before posting any message or photo. Hide phone numbers, and names or faces if she prefers. Never edit her meaning. And prefer specific praise, like the gown was ready two days early.
Your 90-day plan
Build your 90-day plan
Record your starting numbers
Choose one relationship habit
Choose one sales skill
Set three targets for day 90
Check your numbers every month
Finally, your 90-day plan. Record your starting numbers from last month: customers, repeat customers, follow-up rate and referrals.
Choose one relationship habit, written as a clear action. For example, Grace in Abuja follows up with every customer within 2 days of delivery, using a daily 6pm reminder.
Choose one sales skill. Grace asks three open questions before recommending.
Set targets from your own numbers. Grace aims to move repeat customers from 12 of 25 to at least 15 of 25.
Check monthly. If you miss a week, do not abandon the plan. Restart the next day.
Key points
Remember
Thank you, check, reminder, greeting
Cost any reward before you offer it
Ask for referrals when she is happy
Permission for every testimonial
One habit and one skill for 90 days
To remember. Follow up after every sale. Cost any reward before offering it. Ask for referrals at the happy moment, and get permission for every testimonial.
One habit kept for 90 days changes a business more than ten ideas abandoned after a week.
